sources.title: Java Language Specification Chapter 17 Threads and Locks
javap decomposition of exact unsafeIncrement candidate

claims.text: The preserved Java-concurrency Question initializes i to 0 and asks what final values are possible when two threads execute i++ and why; it does not specify extra synchronization, volatile, or atomic wrappers. The answer states the minimal completion/join assumptions explicitly.

Without synchronization, conflicting shared-variable accesses are not ordered by happens-before and constitute a data race; join establishes visibility to the joining thread after worker completion but does not serialize the two worker increments.

The exact unsafeIncrement candidate compiles into distinct shared-field load, integer add, and shared-field store bytecode operations; deterministic legal read/write interleavings demonstrate terminal 1 (lost update) and 2 (serialized updates).
Same-monitor synchronized increments and AtomicInteger atomic increments both produce 2 under the candidate contract in repeated validation.

validation.reported_stdout: PASS synchronized=2 atomic=2 repeats=500 lost-update-interleaving=1 serialized-interleaving=2
checks: unsafeIncrement bytecode contains separate getstatic/iadd/putstatic steps
same-monitor synchronized increments yield 2 in 500 runs

boundary_tests.case: both logical reads see 0 before either write

findings: The answer directly states the 1-or-2 result under explicit ordinary-int/two-completed-thread assumptions instead of hiding prerequisites.
It distinguishes atomic single int access from non-atomic compound i++ and gives both lost-update and serialized interleavings.
The Java memory-model explanation correctly separates worker-worker data race from join-based main-thread completion visibility.
The exact candidate bytecode independently shows load/add/store decomposition; deterministic fixtures witness the two result interleavings without relying on probabilistic scheduler reproduction.
Repeated synchronized and AtomicInteger checks validate both safe alternatives.
The answer avoids the common overclaim that data races permit literally arbitrary int results or that volatile makes compound increment atomic.
